text: Last lesson covered ACID's Isolation property in the abstract: concurrent transactions shouldn't see each other's incomplete work. This lesson is about the actual mechanism SQL Server uses to make that true: locking.

A lock is a flag the engine attaches to a resource — a row, a page, a table — recording that some transaction has a claim on it, and what kind of claim. Every other transaction that wants that same resource has to check in with the lock manager first.

Picture two SSMS windows against AdventureWorks2012. Session A opens a transaction and updates a product's price, but doesn't commit yet. At that instant, Session A is holding an exclusive lock on that one row.

Session B, at the same moment, tries to read that exact row. It doesn't get a half-written value back — it simply waits. The lock manager sees the conflict and blocks Session B until Session A commits or rolls back. That blocking is Isolation, working exactly as designed.

Internally, the lock manager is just a table of who holds what kind of lock on which resource. A compatible request gets granted right away; a conflicting one waits. Different operations ask for different kinds of locks, and the next several lessons walk through each kind in turn: shared, exclusive, update, intent, and schema.

You can't meaningfully turn locking off — without it, Isolation and Consistency fall apart, with readers seeing half-committed writes and writers clobbering each other. Isolation levels, later in this chapter, only adjust how much locking behavior you relax, never remove it. Next up: shared locks, the kind an ordinary SELECT takes.
